assumptions: Steady, incompressible, isothermal, single-phase liquid flow.
Reservoirs and reference nodes are quiescent bodies of liquid (velocity 0) at a constant head.

No entrance or exit loss is applied where a pipe meets a reservoir or reference node unless the connection's piping has an entrance fitting (entrance_sharp, entrance_rounded, entrance_projecting) or an exit fitting (exit); without one, the EGL at the port equals the boundary head in either flow direction. The web app adds a sharp-edged entrance where new piping leaves a reservoir and an exit where it enters one (removable), and none at a reference node; each boundary's trace lists the entrance and exit fittings at its ports.
Fluid properties are constant at the operating temperature.
Pumps have an integral check: no reverse flow.
Check valves: a disc that opens fully above the cracking pressure and closes on reverse flow (no partial opening).
Control valves without an entered resistance are ideal: no loss when fully open.
Fittings and valves without a user K use the cited correlation for the type at the connected pipe's inner diameter.

Relief valves are conventional spring-loaded valves in liquid service, lifting linearly (a convention) from their set pressure difference to full lift at set plus overpressure, with API 520's liquid capacity equation on the total-pressure difference across them.
Equipment losses scale with the square of the flow and with density from one rated point, a Cv or a Kv (constant K); viscosity is not corrected.

Orifice plates meet ISO 5167-2 in geometry and installation; their loss is ISO 5167-2's permanent pressure loss with the discharge coefficient at D and D/2 tappings (or an entered one), for a single-phase liquid.

items: Global Gradient Algorithm (Todini & Pilati 1988): Newton's method on the energy grade line at every node and the flow in every link; sparse direct solve of the Schur complement (SciPy SuperLU, splu). One solver for every topology; every connected part needs a reservoir or reference node.

Converged when the largest flow change is at most the project tolerance times the largest flow (plus 1e-14 m³/s), continuity closes at every node and over every component to 1e-09 x the largest flow + 1e-14 m³/s, and the energy equation holds on every link to 1e-07 m. On each link, 8.88178e-16 x the largest magnitude among the energy grade lines at its two ends and its head loss is added to that tolerance (4 x 2.22045e-16, the machine epsilon of double precision): an allowance for the round-off of the heads that the energy residual subtracts, larger than 1e-07 m only where that magnitude exceeds 1e-07 m divided by that factor, about 1.1259e+08 m.

An active PRV or PSV holds its port's head and passes the flow of the pipe on that port, coupled exactly in Newton's step (EPANET 2.2 lags it by one iteration, which converges the same answer more slowly).
This project: friction method 'colebrook', flow tolerance 1e-09 (relative to the largest flow), at most 100 Newton iterations per network solve.
This solve: 10 Newton iterations in 2 outer iteration(s); converged.

Branch components (tees, wyes) are imposed exactly: each one's ports share one head unknown, offset by the branch's path losses (zero for an ideal junction), and its internal flows follow from continuity.

Flows below 1e-12 x the largest flow (plus 1e-14 m³/s) are round-off and reported as zero. Dead-end branches (no way out but the node they hang from) carry no flow by continuity and are reported as exactly zero.

Outer loop for statuses and branch losses: at most 30 counted iterations; an iteration that only holds or releases branch legs at zero flow is not counted (each branch is held a bounded number of times). Once pump and valve statuses repeat after an iteration that changed several of them, one status changes per iteration; a status pattern that still repeats goes back to the latest iteration that asked for several changes and takes one not yet taken, and with none left is reported as not converged, naming the elements that oscillate.
Parts of the network closed off from every reservoir and reference node by closed elements carry no flow and have no computed pressure (flagged).

A closed-off part that cannot carry zero flow (a pump loop behind a closed valve) has determined flows but no pressure level: its flows and head differences are solved with one node held at an arbitrary head, and its pressures, NPSH available and PRV/PSV setpoint checks are not reported (flagged).

Assigned-flow nodes fix the flow leaving the network at their port (a demand, positive) or entering it (a supply, negative), whatever the pressure there: a nodal demand in the continuity equations, as EPANET's junction demands; their pressure is a result. They are not a fixed-pressure boundary. A dead-end branch to one carries its flow. A part of the network that no reservoir or reference node reaches through open elements carries assigned flows only if they sum to zero (to the continuity tolerance): its flows are then solved and its pressure level is not (flagged); otherwise the closed elements around that part whose status rules open as its pressure falls (a net demand) or rises (a net supply) are re-opened; with none left to open, no steady state carries them, and the solve is reported as not converged, naming the nodes and the elements closed around them (EPANET: a disconnected system). A flow control (an FCV, or a speed-controlled pump) that alone feeds assigned-flow nodes taking its setpoint flow leaves the pressure between them undetermined (reported as not converged, naming them); with another flow the node's flow passes and the control's rules take it to a limit (an FCV fully open below its setpoint, a speed-controlled pump at its maximum or minimum speed), or, above what the control can pass, or with reverse flow through it, no steady state carries it.
references: Todini, E., and S. Pilati. A gradient algorithm for the analysis of pipe networks. Computer Applications in Water Supply, Vol. 1. Wiley, 1988, 1-20.
Rossman, L. A., et al. EPANET 2.2 User Manual. US EPA, 2020 (source: src/hydcoeffs.c).
sections.title: Network solution

items: Darcy–Weisbach head loss h = f (L/D) v²/(2g), g = 9.80665 m/s² (standard gravity, fluids.constants.g), Re = |v| D/ν.
Laminar, Re < 2000: f = 64/Re (Hagen–Poiseuille).
Turbulent, Re ≥ 4000: the Colebrook (1939) equation, solved exactly with fluids.friction.Clamond (Clamond 2009).
Transition, 2000 ≤ Re < 4000: cubic interpolation between the laminar and turbulent laws (Dunlop's method, as in EPANET 2.2); flagged as transitional flow.

Flagged outside the cited range: Swamee–Jain beyond its documented 5000 ≤ Re ≤ 1e+08 and 1e-06 ≤ ε/D ≤ 0.05; Colebrook beyond ε/D = 0.05, the largest relative roughness documented for its explicit approximations (fluids.friction.fmethods). ε/D ≥ 3.7 has no Colebrook solution and is rejected.

Pipe dimensions: ASME B36.10M / B36.19M and ASTM D1785 via fluids.piping; roughness: Farshad & Rieke (2006) via fluids.friction.roughness_Farshad; user values where entered (each element's trace names its sources).
references: Swamee, P. K., and A. K. Jain. J. Hydraulics Div. ASCE 102(5), 1976, 657-664.
Rossman, L. A., et al. EPANET 2.2 User Manual. US EPA, 2020 (source: src/hydcoeffs.c).
sections.title: Pipe friction

items: Fitting loss h = n K v²/(2g), K from the cited fluids correlation for the fitting type (data/fittings.json) at the reference pipe's inner diameter; a user K overrides it.
Crane TP-410 K values use the fully turbulent friction factor ft_Crane(D); they are not valid in laminar flow, and a Crane K in a laminar segment is flagged.
references: Crane Co. TP-410 Flow of Fluids Through Valves, Fittings, and Pipe, 2009.
Rennels, D. C., and H. M. Hudson. Pipe Flow: A Practical and Comprehensive Guide. Wiley, 2012.
sections.title: Minor losses

items: Tees and wyes with lossModel 'ideal' are junctions without loss, as in EPANET.

lossModel 'crane': the path losses follow the solved flow split with the Crane TP-410 tee and lateral correlations (fluids.fittings.K_branch_diverging_Crane, K_run_diverging_Crane, K_branch_converging_Crane, K_run_converging_Crane), K on the combined-flow velocity in the run diameter; updated in the outer loop until K changes by less than 0.0001 and the path loss by less than 1e-06 m.

A tee whose combined flow passes through the branch uses the Darby 3-K tee 'Tee, Through-branch, (as elbow), flanged, (r/D = 1)' per run path on its own velocity (flagged); a wye in that pattern has no cited correlation and is reported as not converged.

Flagged outside the correlations' range: a branch larger than the run (β > 1), unequal run pipes, a wye lateral turning against its lean, and a laminar combined flow (Re < 2000 on the combined-flow velocity in the run diameter: the Crane tee data are for turbulent flow).

Zero flow through a leg: the correlations for flow out through a leg and flow in through it give different port heads in the limit of zero flow. A leg whose flow reverses and reverses back between outer iterations is held at zero flow while the head the network gives its port lies between those two limits; its K is the one its head implies.

A flow split that keeps alternating across a step of a Crane correlation (a split at which the fluids function switches formula, q = 0.4, 0.5 or 0.6, and K jumps by more than 0.0001) holds K at the mean of the fluids values at the two splits while the solved split stays between them (flagged; the trace lists both values); a split alternating where the correlation is continuous has its K update under-relaxed instead.
references: Crane Co. TP-410 Flow of Fluids Through Valves, Fittings, and Pipe, 2009.
Silverberg, P., and R. Darby. Correlate pressure drops through fittings. Chem. Eng. 106(7), 1999, 101.
sections.title: Branches

items: Head, efficiency and NPSHr curves: monotone piecewise cubic interpolation (SciPy PchipInterpolator) through the entered points; head and NPSHr are extrapolated along the end slope outside the points (flagged), efficiency is held at its end values (flagged).
Speed: affinity laws, H(Q) = s² H₀(Q/s), NPSHr(Q) = s² NPSHr₀(Q/s), η(Q) = η₀(Q/s).
No viscosity correction: the curves are used as entered for the fluid (the Hydraulic Institute correction, ANSI/HI 9.6.7, is not in this version).
Integral check: a pump closes when the system head exceeds its shutoff head s² H₀(0) or the flow would reverse (EPANET 2.2 pumpstatus), and is flagged as flow reversal.

System curve of a pump: at each flow the pump is replaced by that fixed flow and the network solved, every other element following its own law and status rules (other pumps keep running); the system head is EGL(discharge) − EGL(suction). Default flows: 0 to 1.2 x the curve's largest flow x s. Each point starts from the solution at the neighbouring flow (statuses, branch losses and flows; the first from the network's own solve when the solve computes the curves, from the initial state otherwise), so where the statuses or branch patterns admit more than one solution the curve follows one continuously; a point that fails from there is solved from the initial state, and one that still has no head while the flow has a way through (unless a control valve in series is at its switch, below) is solved again from the initial state (if it did not start there) and from it with its active control valves open, the first solve that gives a head, or finds a control valve in series at its switch, being used (with none, the point keeps its first result) and the next point starting from the result used; a flowing point is not solved again when its flow exceeds what every way from the pump's discharge back to its suction can pass that way (an FCV at most its setpoint, a check valve, PRV, PSV or pump nothing in reverse: a cut, Ford and Fulkerson), since no steady state carries it, and one whose flow is that limit, where every steady state passes each FCV of the cut at its setpoint, is also solved with each such FCV held open, to find whether it sits at its switch. A point has no head where no steady state carries its flow, where its head is undetermined (a side of the pump with no fixed pressure, or a control valve in series at its switch, which could also hold the flow throttled with any higher head) or where its solve does not converge; its message says which. With assigned-flow nodes, the cut counts their flows as fixed demands and supplies (Gale): a demand on the pump's side of the cut takes part of the forced flow, and one beyond it adds to what the cut must pass. Read the other way, the cut bounds the flow from below: a flowing point below the least flow that assigned flows need through the pump (a demand on its discharge side that a one-way element keeps every reservoir and reference node from feeding, or a supply on its suction side that one keeps from draining) has no steady state either and is not solved again, and one at that floor is solved with each FCV of the cut held open too. A side of the pump that reaches only assigned-flow nodes has no point with a head.
references: Fritsch, F. N., and R. E. Carlson. Monotone piecewise cubic interpolation. SIAM J. Numer. Anal. 17(2), 1980, 238-246.

Fritsch, F. N., and J. Butland. A method for constructing local monotone piecewise cubic interpolants. SIAM J. Sci. Stat. Comput. 5(2), 1984, 300-304, doi:10.1137/0905021 (the derivative formula of scipy.interpolate.PchipInterpolator).
Rossman, L. A., et al. EPANET 2.2. US EPA, 2020 (source: src/hydstatus.c, status rules).

Ford, L. R., and D. R. Fulkerson. Maximal flow through a network. Canadian Journal of Mathematics 8, 1956, 399-404 (the max-flow min-cut theorem: the flows no state carries through a pump on its system curve).

Gale, D. A theorem on flows in networks. Pacific Journal of Mathematics 7(2), 1957, 1073-1082 (a flow with fixed supplies and demands exists when no node set holds more net supply than its cut can pass: the assigned flows in a pump's system-curve bounds).
sections.title: Pumps

items: Open valve loss h = K v²/(2g) on the inlet pipe's inner diameter; Cv and Kv converted with fluids.fittings.Cv_to_K / Kv_to_K (ISA-75.01.01, turbulent flow, without the Reynolds number factor F_R); without a resistance, the Crane TP-410 full-bore K for the valve type. A Cv, Kv or Crane K in laminar flow (Re < 2000 in the inlet pipe) is flagged.

Active check valves: open loss h = Δp_crack/(ρg) + K v²/(2g); open above their cracking head and close on reverse flow (EPANET 2.2 cvstatus with the cracking head). A check valve locked open by the user has the open loss K v²/(2g) only, with no cracking head and no check action; locked closed, it passes no flow.

PRV, PSV and FCV hold the outlet static pressure, inlet static pressure or flow when active; status rules from EPANET 2.2 (hydstatus.c) applied to the energy grade line, with the setpoint head z + p/(ρg) + v²/(2g) at the port; an FCV closes on reverse flow (EPANET's would pass it), and an active FCV opens once the head across it is below its fully open loss at the setpoint (EPANET's waits for a reverse head), as the PRV and PSV rules do. Control valves without a resistance: ideal control valve: no loss when fully open (K = 0); give a resistance for a real valve.
Status tolerances: 0.0001 m in head, 1e-08 m³/s in flow.

An active state with no solution falls back to the states the valve rules give at that solve's first iterations (EPANET 2.2 applies them at every iteration), then to open and closed valves (EPANET's badvalve).

A section closed off by closed pumps or valves carries no flow and has no computed pressure; the closed elements around it are re-tested against the heads it can take at zero flow (a dead-headed pump puts its shutoff head on it), and re-opened when no such head keeps them all closed. A PRV or PSV inside such a section or one whose pressure level is undetermined, or closed between two of them, keeps its state only if one set of section levels holds it together with those closed elements and the other such valves; otherwise the fewest of these elements change, each to the state its rule gives at levels that hold the others (a PRV or PSV that could not be active there, with no fixed head to draw from or deliver to, closes if open and opens if closed).
references: Rossman, L. A., et al. EPANET 2.2. US EPA, 2020 (source: src/hydstatus.c, status rules).
ISA-75.01.01-2007 (60534-2-1 Mod), Flow Equations for Sizing Control Valves.
Crane Co. TP-410 Flow of Fluids Through Valves, Fittings, and Pipe, 2009.
sections.title: Valves

items: Pressure relief valves (conventional spring-loaded, liquid service): the lift x rises linearly from 0 at the set pressure difference Δp_s to 1 at full lift, Δp_f = Δp_s (1 + op), and the flow is API 520's liquid capacity equation at that lift, Q = x Kd A √(2 Δp_t/ρ), in exact SI with Kw = Kc = Kv = 1 (API 520's own form rounds its constant to 11.78, 6.09214e-05 above the exact 11.7792823892, which gives that fraction more area for a flow). Δp_t is the total-pressure difference between the ports, (p_in + ρ v_in²/2) − (p_out + ρ v_out²/2) = ρ g (EGL_in − EGL_out − (z_in − z_out)); on the energy grade line the law is h(Q) = h_set + (Δp(Q) − Δp_s)/(ρ g), h_set = Δp_s/(ρ g) + z_in − z_out, with u = √Δp the largest real root of u³ − Δp_s u − R Q = 0 between set and full lift (R = (Δp_f − Δp_s)/(Kd A √(2/ρ)); the increment R Q/u and its slope computed without cancellation) and Δp = ρ Q²/(2 (Kd A)²) from full lift on. h is continuous and strictly increasing, with a finite positive slope at zero flow.

Three named departures. (1) The band between set and full lift is a convention, the linear lift of MathWorks Simscape and AFT Impulse, exact at the two points the certification fixes, not the cited behaviour: Pentair's typical liquid-trim characteristic (TP-V300 Fig. 4-12) lifts to about half at 107 % of set, surges to full lift there, and on falling pressure stays at full lift to about 95 % and recloses near 90 %, so between about 90 % and 107 % of set a real valve has two steady states; a valve that has surged open passes more flow at a lower inlet pressure. No cited source verifies a band law, so every relieving state short of full lift is flagged (CORRELATION_OUT_OF_RANGE, partial lift), and the band is an exception to the project's verifiable gate that the owner accepted (CLAUDE.md D21). (2) API 520's P1 − P2 is read as Δp_t; ASME's definitions as Pentair quotes them (the inlet stagnation pressure, the outlet static pressure) differ by the outlet velocity head, and this reading gives the higher inlet pressure at a given flow. (3) With a superimposed back pressure the overpressure is taken on the set difference, as the opening is, so full lift comes op × the back pressure below the in-situ relieving pressure; at the relieving pressure both readings are at or past full lift and give API 520's flow.

Overpressure at full lift: ASME's liquid certification overpressure, 10 % of the set or 3 psi (20684.3 Pa), whichever is greater (the default), ASME VIII's liquid certification overpressure, for a set of at least 15 psi (103421 Pa), ASME VIII's scope; a certified capacity may give its own. Below that scope the default is not cited: a valve that would take it is refused (RELIEF_VALVE_OUT_OF_RANGE), with the remedy of a certified capacity and its overpressure.

Capacity, one of three kinds, never mixed: an API 526 orifice letter (its effective area) or an API 520 effective area, each with API 520's effective coefficient of discharge 0.65 and ASME's overpressure, for preliminary sizing (an effective area is reported with the smallest API 526 letter covering it, fluids.safety_valve.API520_round_size); or the valve's certified actual orifice area with its rated coefficient of discharge (ASME's K, 0.9 × the measured coefficient) and, optionally, its full-lift overpressure. Pentair: never an effective coefficient or area with a rated coefficient or actual area.

Status: active, or locked closed (gagged, or isolated by its block valve). Its status rule is the check valve's (EPANET 2.2 cvstatus) with the cracking head h_set: at zero flow it opens once the static pressure difference across it exceeds its set by ρ g × 0.0001 m, and it closes on reverse flow. It starts closed, its normal state (a pump deadheaded behind a valve set above its shutoff then runs at zero flow with its shutoff pressure on the inlet). A check valve's cracking pressure, unlike the relief valve's set, is compared with the difference of the energy grade lines. Every closed-off, free-level and system-curve rule applies to it as to a check valve (in a pump's system curve it passes no reverse flow). A point of a pump's system curve, where the pump is a fixed flow, starts it open, as a check valve, so that the flow has its way through it and its rule closes it where the difference across it stays below its set; at zero flow it then sits at its set, H_sys(0) holding h_set.

Flagged: full lift (RELIEF_VALVE_OPEN, information); relieving short of full lift (CORRELATION_OUT_OF_RANGE, partial lift, warning); an active valve closed with a side closed off or on an undetermined level, which has no result (RELIEF_VALVE_CLOSED, information, naming the levels that keep it closed); an outlet whose absolute static pressure is below the vapor pressure while it relieves (BELOW_VAPOR_PRESSURE: the jet would flash, and the flow solved is too high); a liquid of viscosity 0.1 Pa·s or more (CORRELATION_OUT_OF_RANGE, viscosity: API 520's Kv, given in the trace, is not applied). Refused (RELIEF_VALVE_OUT_OF_RANGE): a law the floating point cannot represent (Kd A, Q_f or R not a finite positive normal number), and a set below ASME VIII's scope with ASME's default overpressure.

Not applied: API 520's back-pressure correction Kw (a conventional valve's set is the difference across it), its rupture-disc combination factor Kc and its viscosity correction Kv; no blowdown or pop action; the outlet piping is liquid-full.
references: API Standard 520, Sizing, Selection, and Installation of Pressure-relieving Devices, Part I, Sizing and Selection, 10th edition: the liquid capacity equation for a valve certified for liquid service, with the effective coefficient of discharge 0.65 for preliminary sizing and the viscosity correction Kv (not read: via fluids 1.3.1 fluids.safety_valve.API520_A_l, its raw expression in SI units, and API520_Kv; and the Pentair handbook).

API Standard 526, Flanged Steel Pressure-relief Valves: the effective orifice areas of the letters D to T (not read: via fluids 1.3.1 fluids.safety_valve.API526_A, API526_letters and API520_round_size, and Pentair TP-V300 Table 7-6).

Pentair, Pressure Relief Valve Engineering Handbook, Technical Publication No. TP-V300, rev. 12-2012 (a secondary source on ASME Section VIII, API 520 and API 526): the definitions of set pressure, overpressure, relieving pressure and back pressure (ch. 2); ASME's liquid certification overpressure, 10 % or 3 psi (ch. 3, p. 3.15); a conventional valve's bench setting and the back pressure on its disc (ch. 4); the typical relief valve lift characteristic, Fig. 4-12 (ch. 4, p. 4.8); ASME VIII's scope, set pressures of 15 psig and above (ch. 5, p. 5.3); rated K = 0.9 × the measured coefficient and the rule never to mix API's effective values with a valve's rated values (ch. 5); Table 7-6 (ch. 7).
MathWorks. Simscape Fluids, Pressure Relief Valve (IL) block: the valve opens linearly from its set pressure over its pressure regulation range to fully open.
Applied Flow Technology. AFT Impulse help, relief valve: the valve opens from its set pressure to fully open at its full-open overpressure (linear in between).
Rossman, L. A., et al. EPANET 2.2. US EPA, 2020 (source: src/hydstatus.c, status rules).
OpenSolve Pipe design decision D21 (CLAUDE.md), from docs/proposals/pressure-relief-valve.md (the owner's answers of 2026-10-28: the linear lift in the band, an exception to GOALS §5).
sections.title: Relief valves

items: Equipment (one side of a heat exchanger, a coil, a strainer, a filter, or another passive element given by its datasheet): the loss of total head from its inlet to its outlet is h = EGL_in − EGL_out = c Q|Q| (a loss of total pressure ρ g h), with c = ΔP_r/(ρ_r g Q_r²) from the rated pressure drop ΔP_r at the rated flow Q_r for a fluid of density ρ_r: a constant K, the square law of ISA-75.01.01-2007 eq. (1) for non-choked, turbulent liquid flow, and the high-Re limit of the 3-K method (Silverberg & Darby). The rated drop is the dissipative loss (friction and form) of total pressure between the ports, without the static head between them: each port's static pressure follows from its EGL with the velocity in its connected pipe, so the static drop reported is ρ g h + ρ g (z_out − z_in) + ρ (v_out² − v_in²)/2.

Density scaling: the pressure loss at the solved flow is ρ g h = ΔP_r (ρ/ρ_r)(Q/Q_r)², with ρ the fluid being solved. The operating density cancels out of the head loss h, which the rating alone sets; it only converts head to pressure.

A Cv or Kv rating is a rated point on water by definition (1 psi at Cv US gpm, 1 bar at Kv m³/h): c = K/(2 g A²) with K from fluids.fittings.Cv_to_K / Kv_to_K (ISA-75.01.01-2007, water at 999.29744568 kg/m³), the valves' conversion, evaluated at a 1 m bore; K ∝ D⁴ makes K/A² the same on every bore, so no pipe diameter is needed. Its pressure loss is (ρ/ρ_w) × 1 psi × (Q/Cv gpm)², or × 1 bar × (Q/Kv m³/h)².
Reverse flow (outlet → inlet) follows the same, symmetric law and is flagged: no datasheet rates reverse flow.
Laminar flow (Re < 2000) in the end segment of a connected pipe is flagged, as for a valve's Cv or Kv: the square law is the turbulent-flow law, and the loss is then likely underestimated.

At zero flow the law's slope 2c|Q| is 0: Newton's Jacobian uses at least 1e-06 x the slopes of the pipes at the element's ports there, as for every link that is not a pipe (EPANET 2.2 bounds such a gradient instead); the law itself is exact.

Viscosity is not corrected: the loss scales with density only. With a fluid more viscous than the rating's, or at flows well below the rated flow, the real loss may be higher than this law gives (a smooth-tube element dominated by friction scales as ρ^0.75 μ^0.25 Q^1.75 by Blasius' law); a correction needs the equipment's geometry or its vendor's own factors.
references: ISA-75.01.01-2007 (60534-2-1 Mod), Flow Equations for Sizing Control Valves.
Silverberg, P., and R. Darby. Correlate pressure drops through fittings. Chem. Eng. 106(7), 1999, 101.
sections.title: Equipment

items: Orifice plates (square-edged, concentric; a restriction orifice, or a flow meter with pressure taps): the loss of total head from the inlet to the outlet is h = EGL_in − EGL_out = K v|v|/(2g), with v = Q/A in the inlet pipe of inner diameter D (its end segment at the inlet port), β = d/D, and K = (S/(C β²) − 1)², S = √(1 − β⁴(1 − C²)): ISO 5167-2's pressure-loss relation Δϖ = (S − C β²)/(S + C β²) × Δp over ρ v²/2 (fluids.flow_meter.discharge_coefficient_to_K, computed without its cancellation as β → 1). Δϖ = ρ g h is the permanent pressure loss, the part not recovered about 6 D downstream; the outlet port's pressure is the recovered one.

The discharge coefficient C that sets the loss is the one at D and D/2 tappings for every plate, whatever its own taps: ISO 5167-2:2003 eq. (4), the Reader-Harris/Gallagher equation (fluids.flow_meter.C_Reader_Harris_Gallagher), at Re_D = 4ρ|Q|/(πDμ) in the inlet pipe. One plate has one permanent loss; the loss relation's theory (Reader-Harris et al. 2019) takes C with tappings 1D upstream, and of ISO's tap sets only D and D/2 has L1 = 1 (Deltares WANDA makes the same choice). Named departures, each at its largest over ISO 5167-2's range (D 50 mm to 1 m, β 0.1 to 0.75, Re_D from Re_lo up): ISO's relation read with a meter's own C would give a K up to 6.14 % higher at corner tappings and 6.34 % at flange tappings (at β 0.75 as Re_D grows, flange on a 1 m pipe), a flow up to 2.94 % and 3.03 % lower where the plate takes the whole head (up to β 0.6: a K up to 0.64 % and 0.84 % higher, a flow up to 0.32 % and 0.42 % lower); Reader-Harris et al.'s own C, with the downstream pressure at 0.125 D, gives a K 0.063 to 1.24 % lower (a flow up to 0.63 % higher).

Below ISO 5167-2's lowest Reynolds number Re_lo, C is held at its value there and flagged (WANDA's practice; eq. (4) as written exceeds 1 at very low Re): Re_lo = max(5000, 16000 β²) at corner and D and D/2 tappings and max(5000, 170000 β² D) at flange tappings (D in m). The first is ISO's limit (5000 for β ≤ 0.56, 16000 β² above) made continuous at β 0.56, stricter by at most 17.6 for 0.559 < β < 0.56, so that the held loss decreases with β. So fluids is never evaluated below Re 5000, where it adds terms that are not in ISO 5167-2.

A plate whose coefficient that sets the loss, at D and D/2 tappings (ISO's C there, or an entered C moved there from corner or flange taps), could exceed 1 at some flow is refused (ORIFICE_OUT_OF_RANGE): C ≤ 1 is a jet no larger than the bore, and above it K falls below the sudden expansion from the bore (Borda-Carnot), which is physically impossible. So is a plate whose ISO coefficient could exceed 1 where eq. (4) serves only the reading or the move: at its corner or flange tappings for ISO's meter reading, or at either tap set in the ratio that moves an entered C. Eq. (4) is then extrapolated far beyond ISO's range (its largest C there is below 0.7), and the reading or the move would rest on it. Each bound takes each Reynolds-number-dependent term of eq. (4) at whichever end of [Re_lo, ∞) makes it safe. For ISO's C it refuses β from about 0.970 (0.97025 from D 71.12 mm, at most 0.9706 on smaller pipes), and with flange taps on a pipe below about 55 mm, where ISO's C at the flange tappings is the bound, from a lower β (0.969 at D 52.5 mm, 0.963 at 40.9 mm, 0.930 at 15.8 mm, lower still on smaller pipes). A plate whose loss coefficient K/(2 g A²) at its smallest C is not a finite positive floating-point number is refused too.

A meter's reading, the differential pressure between its taps, is ISO 5167-2 eq. (1) solved for Δp with ε = 1: Δp = (1 − β⁴)/(C_M² β⁴) · ρ v|v|/2, with C_M ISO's C at its own taps (held at their own Re_lo) or the entered C; it does not act on the network. A plate without taps (a restriction orifice) has no reading.

The static pressure at the vena contracta, p_vc = p_up + ρ g (z_up − z_down) − (1 − β⁴)/(C² β⁴) · ρ v²/2 (up: the port the flow enters; down: the port it leaves by, at whose elevation it is taken, as in WANDA), is checked against the vapor pressure and flagged where the liquid would flash (BELOW_VAPOR_PRESSURE): a flashing jet chokes the flow, so the flow solved is then too high. None at zero flow or where the pressure level is undetermined; incipient cavitation is not checked.

Flagged (CORRELATION_OUT_OF_RANGE), wherever eq. (4) is used: a bore below 12.5 mm, an inlet pipe outside 50 mm to 1000 mm, β outside 0.1 to 0.75 (ISO 5167-2's limits, from fluids' documentation); and for every plate, an outlet pipe of another bore than the inlet's (the relation assumes the jet recovers in the same bore) and reverse flow (the loss taken as for forward flow at the same flow rate: ISO's C is for flow onto the plate's upstream face). The plate and its installation (edge, thickness, straight lengths, roughness) are assumed to meet ISO 5167-2 and are not checked.

At zero flow the law's slope is 0: Newton's Jacobian uses at least 1e-06 x the slopes of the pipes at the plate's ports there, as for every link that is not a pipe; the law itself is exact. Elsewhere the slope is exact, with the derivative of eq. (4) in the Reynolds number.
ε = 1: the expansibility factor of a liquid.
references: ISO 5167-2:2003, Measurement of fluid flow by means of pressure differential devices inserted in circular cross-section conduits running full, Part 2: Orifice plates; eq. (1), eq. (4) (the Reader-Harris/Gallagher (1998) equation) and the pressure-loss relation, as fluids 1.3.1 implements them (fluids.flow_meter), with its limits from fluids' docstrings (also citing ASME MFC-3M-2004). The 2022 edition does not change eq. (4) or its limits (Reader-Harris, M. J. ISO 5167: Past and Present. Global Flow Measurement Workshop, 2022).

FLOMEKO 2019, Lisbon (the loss relation's momentum theory, C taken with tappings 1D upstream and between the plate and the vena contracta downstream, and pressures moved between tap positions with the Reader-Harris/Gallagher (1998) equation).

Deltares. WANDA documentation, ORIFICE component (an orifice plate complying with ISO 5167-2:2003): the loss H1 − H2 for D and D/2 tappings, the Reynolds number held at the standard's minimum, symmetric reverse flow, and the vena-contracta pressure at the downstream side's elevation.

equations: Q_in = Q_a: continuity at the port (Q_in: the flow into the node through its connection; with a supply, Q_a < 0, the connection carries the flow away)
EGL: solved with the network (the port is a free node: its pressure is a result, not an input)
v = |Q_in|/A: velocity in the pipe connected at the port (its end segment, area A)
HGL = EGL − v²/(2g)
p = ρ g (EGL − z_port − v²/(2g)): static gauge pressure at a port (z_port: the port's elevation; v: the velocity in the pipe connected there, Q/A of its end segment)
p_abs = p + p_atm (checked against the vapor pressure)

inputs.name: Assigned flow Q_a (positive: leaves the network, a demand; negative: enters it, a supply)

intermediates.name: Flow into the node through its connection Q_in

notes: Assigned-flow node: it fixes the flow at its port whatever the pressure there. It is not a fixed-pressure boundary: a part of the network that no reservoir or reference node reaches through open elements (cut off by a closed valve or a stopped pump, say) carries a nonzero flow only if the assigned flows there sum to zero, and then its flows are solved and its pressure level is not (UNDETERMINED_PRESSURE); otherwise no steady state carries them, and the solve is reported as not converged, naming the node. A zero flow there is a closed end (ISOLATED_SECTION).

equations: h_r = ΔP_r/(ρ_r g): the rated head loss
c = h_r/Q_r²: the loss coefficient
EGL_in − EGL_out = h = c Q|Q| = h_r (Q/Q_r)|Q/Q_r| (Q: flow inlet → outlet)
ρ g h = ΔP_r (ρ/ρ_r)(Q/Q_r)|Q/Q_r|: the pressure loss at the solved flow and the case fluid's density ρ
A = π D²/4, v = Q/A and Re = |v| D/ν in the end segment of the pipe connected at each port (ν = μ/ρ)
p_in = ρ g (EGL_in − z_in − v_in²/(2g)), p_out = ρ g (EGL_out − z_out − v_out²/(2g)): static gauge pressures at the ports
Δp_static = p_in − p_out = ρ g h + ρ g (z_out − z_in) + ρ (v_out² − v_in²)/2: the static pressure drop

inputs.name: Rated pressure drop ΔP_r (loss of total pressure, inlet → outlet)
Inlet pipe inner diameter (its end segment at the port)
Outlet pipe inner diameter (its end segment at the port)

intermediates.name: Rated head loss h_r = ΔP_r/(ρ_r g)
Head loss by the law c Q|Q|
Static pressure drop Δp_static = p_in − p_out

notes: Scenario 'Cv valve' (id S1) overrides the base project here: rated pressure drop 40000 Pa (base: 20000 Pa). The inputs below are the scenario's values.

The rated drop is the dissipative loss of total pressure between the ports (friction and form), without the static head between them: the law acts on the energy grade line, and each port's static pressure follows from its EGL with the velocity in the pipe connected there, so the static drop also holds the ports' elevation and velocity-head terms. A datasheet's static drop S between nozzles at different elevations or bores is entered as S − ρ_r g (z_out − z_in) − ρ_r (v_out² − v_in²)/2, with the ports at their real elevations.

The loss scales with density only. It does not account for a viscosity or Reynolds number different from the datasheet's: with a more viscous fluid, or at flows well below the rated flow, the real loss may be higher than this law gives.

Density ratio ρ/ρ_r = 0.9991037252: the case fluid (998.2071505 kg/m³) is lighter than the fluid the rating is for (999.102621 kg/m³), so at any flow the pressure loss is 0.9991037252 × ΔP_r (Q/Q_r)²; the head loss does not depend on the density.

equations: H = z_port + p/(ρ g): the EGL held at the port (an ideal boundary: a body of liquid at rest at gauge pressure p)
Q_out = flow from the reference node into the network
notes: Ideal reference node: it supplies or takes any flow at its fixed pressure (velocity 0 at the boundary).

No entrance or exit loss is applied where a pipe meets this boundary unless the connection's piping has an entrance fitting (entrance_sharp, entrance_rounded, entrance_projecting: the loss where flow leaves the boundary into the pipe) or an exit fitting (exit: the loss where flow leaves the pipe into the boundary). Without one, the EGL at the port equals the boundary head H in either flow direction: the velocity head v²/(2g) of the connected pipe is gained on entry and given back on exit with no loss. Such a fitting is a loss of its connection (see that connection's trace). The web app adds a sharp-edged entrance (entrance_sharp) where new piping leaves a reservoir and an exit where it enters one, which the user can remove; it adds none at a reference node.
Port port_1, connection 'L10': its piping has exit fitting(s) exit.

notes: Scenario 'Cv valve' (id S1) overrides the base project here: bore diameter 0.03 m (base: 0.025 m). The inputs below are the scenario's values.

One loss per plate: the loss uses the discharge coefficient at D and D/2 tappings whatever the plate's own taps (proposal orifice-plate.md decision 5), since one plate has one permanent loss, which cannot depend on where a meter's taps were drilled. The pressure-loss relation's theory (Reader-Harris et al. 2019) takes C with tappings 1D upstream and between the plate and the vena contracta downstream; of ISO 5167-2's tap sets only D and D/2 has L1 = 1, and Deltares WANDA uses it for its whole element. This departs from ISO's relation read literally with a meter's own C, which over ISO 5167-2's range (D 50 mm to 1 m, β 0.1 to 0.75, Re_D from Re_lo up) gives a K up to 6.14 % higher at corner tappings and 6.34 % at flange tappings, both at β 0.75 as Re_D grows (flange on a 1 m pipe): a flow up to 2.94 % and 3.03 % lower where the plate takes the whole head; up to β 0.6, a K up to 0.64 % and 0.84 % higher (a flow up to 0.32 % and 0.42 % lower).

Reader-Harris et al. 2019 take the downstream pressure at 0.125 D (L1 = 1, L2' = 0.125) for that C; over ISO 5167-2's range their C gives a K 0.063 to 1.24 % lower than D and D/2's (a flow up to 0.63 % higher where the plate takes the whole head). D and D/2 is kept: an ISO tap set, with ISO's own Reynolds number limits. The alternative's C and K at this plate are shown above, not used.

The plate and its installation are assumed to meet ISO 5167-2 (a square-edged concentric plate, its edge and thickness, straight lengths, pipe roughness): they are not checked, nor are fluids' 250 kPa differential-pressure and 6 micrometre roughness limits. d and D are taken at flowing conditions (thermal expansion is not modelled). ε = 1: the expansibility factor of a liquid.

The outlet port's pressure is the recovered one: ISO 5167-2's permanent loss is the part of the pressure difference across the plate not recovered about 6 D downstream (fluids; Reader-Harris et al. 2019's momentum balance), in a pipe of the inlet's bore.

The vena contracta is taken at the elevation of the port the flow leaves by (Deltares WANDA): p_vc = p_up + ρ g (z_up − z_down) − (1 − β⁴)/(C_L² β⁴) ρ v²/2, with p_up the static pressure of the port the flow enters. At zero flow there is no jet: no p_vc, nothing checked. Flashing there is flagged (BELOW_VAPOR_PRESSURE); incipient cavitation is not checked.

Flag CORRELATION_OUT_OF_RANGE (warning): orifice 'O1': its outlet pipe diameter 0.0627 m differs from its inlet pipe diameter 0.05 m; ISO 5167-2's pressure-loss relation assumes the jet recovers in a pipe of the inlet's bore, about 6 D downstream, so the loss is less certain

notes: Quiescent boundary: the liquid level is constant and the liquid at rest (velocity 0); velocity head develops in the connected pipes.

No entrance or exit loss is applied where a pipe meets this boundary unless the connection's piping has an entrance fitting (entrance_sharp, entrance_rounded, entrance_projecting: the loss where flow leaves the boundary into the pipe) or an exit fitting (exit: the loss where flow leaves the pipe into the boundary). Without one, the EGL at the port equals the boundary head H in either flow direction: the velocity head v²/(2g) of the connected pipe is gained on entry and given back on exit with no loss. Such a fitting is a loss of its connection (see that connection's trace). The web app adds a sharp-edged entrance (entrance_sharp) where new piping leaves a reservoir and an exit where it enters one, which the user can remove; it adds none at a reference node.

notes: Scenario 'Cv valve' (id S1) overrides the base project here: set pressure 270000 Pa (base: 350000 Pa); API 526 orifice letter K (base: J). The inputs below are the scenario's values.
ASME's default overpressure at this set is its 10 %, 3 psi/Δp_s = 20684.27188/270000 = 0.07660841437 < 0.1: op = 0.1.

Preliminary: API 520's effective values (API 526's effective area or an API 520 effective area, with the effective coefficient of discharge 0.65), for preliminary sizing; the selected valve's actual area and rated coefficient give its capacity.

Open, partial lift (x = 0.8038801302): the difference across it has not fallen below its set by more than ρ g Htol, EGL_in − EGL_out = 29.79903286 m ≥ h_set − Htol = 27.58168775 m, and Q = 0.01497938597 m³/s ≥ −Qtol = -1e-08 m³/s (EPANET 2.2 cvstatus with the cracking head h_set).

A conventional spring-loaded valve: its spring sees the pressure difference across the disc, so a back pressure adds to the inlet pressure at which it opens. Its set pressure is the static pressure difference, inlet minus outlet, at which it starts to open: discharging to atmosphere at the valve's elevation, the gauge set pressure; against a constant back pressure, the bench setting (the set pressure minus that back pressure, Pentair TP-V300 ch. 4). It opens on the static difference, where a check valve's cracking pressure reads the difference of the energy grade lines.

The overpressure is taken on the set difference, as the opening is: with a superimposed back pressure P_b, full lift comes op · P_b below the in-situ relieving pressure, (1 + op) × the gauge set. ASME's certification fixes full lift only on the bench, discharging to atmosphere, where the two coincide; for full lift against a back pressure this is an inference (proposal pressure-relief-valve.md §1.1), named. At the relieving pressure both readings are at or past full lift and give API 520's flow.

Between set and full lift the lift rises linearly with the overpressure: a convention (MathWorks Simscape, AFT Impulse), exact at the two points the certification fixes, not a cited law, and every relieving state short of full lift is flagged. Pentair's typical liquid-trim lift characteristic (TP-V300 Fig. 4-12) lifts to about half at 107 % of set, surges to full lift there, and on falling pressure stays at full lift to about 95 % and recloses near 90 % (a fixed blowdown of 10 to 15 %). This state is on a rising branch; a valve that has surged open passes more flow at a lower inlet pressure.

What the certification does not bound: ASME VIII's set tolerance (±2 psi to 70 psig, ±3 % above, Pentair TP-V300 Table 3-2), and a rated coefficient that is 0.9 × the measured one, so a certified valve's capacity may exceed its rated capacity.

API 520's P1 − P2 is read as the total-pressure difference between the ports (the law's Δp_t). ASME's definitions as Pentair quotes them put the capacity on the inlet stagnation pressure and the outlet static pressure, which differs from Δp_t by the outlet velocity head; the static reading differs by the difference of the two velocity heads. The differences and flows of both other readings at the solved pressures are shown above, not used.

Kw = Kc = Kv = 1 (no back-pressure, rupture-disc or viscosity correction); no blowdown or pop action; the outlet piping is liquid-full (an outlet pipe rising or falling to an open end adds its static head to the opening pressure); liquids only.
μ = 0.001001596143 Pa·s < 0.1 Pa·s: API 520 recommends Kv = 1 (as fluids documents it).

Flag CORRELATION_OUT_OF_RANGE (warning): relief valve 'RV1' relieves at partial lift (0.80388): between set and full lift the lift is the linear convention, not a cited law. A typical liquid-trim valve lifts more slowly, surges to full lift near 107 % of set and recloses near 90 % (Pentair TP-V300 Fig. 4-12). A valve that has surged open passes more flow at a lower inlet pressure.

equations: Σ Q_port = 0: continuity (port flows positive into the component)
p = ρ g (EGL − z_port − v²/(2g)): static gauge pressure at a port (z_port: the port's elevation; v: the velocity in the pipe connected there, Q/A of its end segment)
q = Q_branch/Q_c: the branch's share of the combined flow Q_c (the flow through the one port that carries all of it)
β = D_branch/D_run (D_run: pipe on the combined port)
v_c = Q_c/A_run, A_run = π D_run²/4: the combined-flow velocity
h_path = K_path v_c²/(2g): the loss between the combined port and each other port, K_path from the Crane correlation for the pattern
EGL_port = EGL_combined − h_path (diverging) or EGL_combined + h_path (converging)
notes: Solved flow pattern: diverging from run_inlet.

assumptions: Steady, incompressible, isothermal, single-phase liquid flow.
Reservoirs and reference nodes are quiescent bodies of liquid (velocity 0) at a constant head.

No entrance or exit loss is applied where a pipe meets a reservoir or reference node unless the connection's piping has an entrance fitting (entrance_sharp, entrance_rounded, entrance_projecting) or an exit fitting (exit); without one, the EGL at the port equals the boundary head in either flow direction. The web app adds a sharp-edged entrance where new piping leaves a reservoir and an exit where it enters one (removable), and none at a reference node; each boundary's trace lists the entrance and exit fittings at its ports.
Fluid properties are constant at the operating temperature.
Pumps have an integral check: no reverse flow.
Check valves: a disc that opens fully above the cracking pressure and closes on reverse flow (no partial opening).
Control valves without an entered resistance are ideal: no loss when fully open.
Fittings and valves without a user K use the cited correlation for the type at the connected pipe's inner diameter.

Relief valves are conventional spring-loaded valves in liquid service, lifting linearly (a convention) from their set pressure difference to full lift at set plus overpressure, with API 520's liquid capacity equation on the total-pressure difference across them.
Equipment losses scale with the square of the flow and with density from one rated point, a Cv or a Kv (constant K); viscosity is not corrected.

Orifice plates meet ISO 5167-2 in geometry and installation; their loss is ISO 5167-2's permanent pressure loss with the discharge coefficient at D and D/2 tappings (or an entered one), for a single-phase liquid.

sections.title: Scenario

items: Global Gradient Algorithm (Todini & Pilati 1988): Newton's method on the energy grade line at every node and the flow in every link; sparse direct solve of the Schur complement (SciPy SuperLU, splu). One solver for every topology; every connected part needs a reservoir or reference node.

Converged when the largest flow change is at most the project tolerance times the largest flow (plus 1e-14 m³/s), continuity closes at every node and over every component to 1e-09 x the largest flow + 1e-14 m³/s, and the energy equation holds on every link to 1e-07 m. On each link, 8.88178e-16 x the largest magnitude among the energy grade lines at its two ends and its head loss is added to that tolerance (4 x 2.22045e-16, the machine epsilon of double precision): an allowance for the round-off of the heads that the energy residual subtracts, larger than 1e-07 m only where that magnitude exceeds 1e-07 m divided by that factor, about 1.1259e+08 m.

An active PRV or PSV holds its port's head and passes the flow of the pipe on that port, coupled exactly in Newton's step (EPANET 2.2 lags it by one iteration, which converges the same answer more slowly).
This project: friction method 'colebrook', flow tolerance 1e-09 (relative to the largest flow), at most 100 Newton iterations per network solve.
This solve: 15 Newton iterations in 2 outer iteration(s); converged.

Branch components (tees, wyes) are imposed exactly: each one's ports share one head unknown, offset by the branch's path losses (zero for an ideal junction), and its internal flows follow from continuity.

Flows below 1e-12 x the largest flow (plus 1e-14 m³/s) are round-off and reported as zero. Dead-end branches (no way out but the node they hang from) carry no flow by continuity and are reported as exactly zero.

Outer loop for statuses and branch losses: at most 30 counted iterations; an iteration that only holds or releases branch legs at zero flow is not counted (each branch is held a bounded number of times). Once pump and valve statuses repeat after an iteration that changed several of them, one status changes per iteration; a status pattern that still repeats goes back to the latest iteration that asked for several changes and takes one not yet taken, and with none left is reported as not converged, naming the elements that oscillate.
Parts of the network closed off from every reservoir and reference node by closed elements carry no flow and have no computed pressure (flagged).

A closed-off part that cannot carry zero flow (a pump loop behind a closed valve) has determined flows but no pressure level: its flows and head differences are solved with one node held at an arbitrary head, and its pressures, NPSH available and PRV/PSV setpoint checks are not reported (flagged).

Assigned-flow nodes fix the flow leaving the network at their port (a demand, positive) or entering it (a supply, negative), whatever the pressure there: a nodal demand in the continuity equations, as EPANET's junction demands; their pressure is a result. They are not a fixed-pressure boundary. A dead-end branch to one carries its flow. A part of the network that no reservoir or reference node reaches through open elements carries assigned flows only if they sum to zero (to the continuity tolerance): its flows are then solved and its pressure level is not (flagged); otherwise the closed elements around that part whose status rules open as its pressure falls (a net demand) or rises (a net supply) are re-opened; with none left to open, no steady state carries them, and the solve is reported as not converged, naming the nodes and the elements closed around them (EPANET: a disconnected system). A flow control (an FCV, or a speed-controlled pump) that alone feeds assigned-flow nodes taking its setpoint flow leaves the pressure between them undetermined (reported as not converged, naming them); with another flow the node's flow passes and the control's rules take it to a limit (an FCV fully open below its setpoint, a speed-controlled pump at its maximum or minimum speed), or, above what the control can pass, or with reverse flow through it, no steady state carries it.
references: Todini, E., and S. Pilati. A gradient algorithm for the analysis of pipe networks. Computer Applications in Water Supply, Vol. 1. Wiley, 1988, 1-20.
Rossman, L. A., et al. EPANET 2.2 User Manual. US EPA, 2020 (source: src/hydcoeffs.c).
sections.title: Network solution

items: Darcy–Weisbach head loss h = f (L/D) v²/(2g), g = 9.80665 m/s² (standard gravity, fluids.constants.g), Re = |v| D/ν.
Laminar, Re < 2000: f = 64/Re (Hagen–Poiseuille).
Turbulent, Re ≥ 4000: the Colebrook (1939) equation, solved exactly with fluids.friction.Clamond (Clamond 2009).
Transition, 2000 ≤ Re < 4000: cubic interpolation between the laminar and turbulent laws (Dunlop's method, as in EPANET 2.2); flagged as transitional flow.

Flagged outside the cited range: Swamee–Jain beyond its documented 5000 ≤ Re ≤ 1e+08 and 1e-06 ≤ ε/D ≤ 0.05; Colebrook beyond ε/D = 0.05, the largest relative roughness documented for its explicit approximations (fluids.friction.fmethods). ε/D ≥ 3.7 has no Colebrook solution and is rejected.

Pipe dimensions: ASME B36.10M / B36.19M and ASTM D1785 via fluids.piping; roughness: Farshad & Rieke (2006) via fluids.friction.roughness_Farshad; user values where entered (each element's trace names its sources).
references: Swamee, P. K., and A. K. Jain. J. Hydraulics Div. ASCE 102(5), 1976, 657-664.
Rossman, L. A., et al. EPANET 2.2 User Manual. US EPA, 2020 (source: src/hydcoeffs.c).
sections.title: Pipe friction

items: Fitting loss h = n K v²/(2g), K from the cited fluids correlation for the fitting type (data/fittings.json) at the reference pipe's inner diameter; a user K overrides it.
Crane TP-410 K values use the fully turbulent friction factor ft_Crane(D); they are not valid in laminar flow, and a Crane K in a laminar segment is flagged.
references: Crane Co. TP-410 Flow of Fluids Through Valves, Fittings, and Pipe, 2009.
Rennels, D. C., and H. M. Hudson. Pipe Flow: A Practical and Comprehensive Guide. Wiley, 2012.
sections.title: Minor losses

items: Tees and wyes with lossModel 'ideal' are junctions without loss, as in EPANET.

lossModel 'crane': the path losses follow the solved flow split with the Crane TP-410 tee and lateral correlations (fluids.fittings.K_branch_diverging_Crane, K_run_diverging_Crane, K_branch_converging_Crane, K_run_converging_Crane), K on the combined-flow velocity in the run diameter; updated in the outer loop until K changes by less than 0.0001 and the path loss by less than 1e-06 m.

A tee whose combined flow passes through the branch uses the Darby 3-K tee 'Tee, Through-branch, (as elbow), flanged, (r/D = 1)' per run path on its own velocity (flagged); a wye in that pattern has no cited correlation and is reported as not converged.

Flagged outside the correlations' range: a branch larger than the run (β > 1), unequal run pipes, a wye lateral turning against its lean, and a laminar combined flow (Re < 2000 on the combined-flow velocity in the run diameter: the Crane tee data are for turbulent flow).

Zero flow through a leg: the correlations for flow out through a leg and flow in through it give different port heads in the limit of zero flow. A leg whose flow reverses and reverses back between outer iterations is held at zero flow while the head the network gives its port lies between those two limits; its K is the one its head implies.

A flow split that keeps alternating across a step of a Crane correlation (a split at which the fluids function switches formula, q = 0.4, 0.5 or 0.6, and K jumps by more than 0.0001) holds K at the mean of the fluids values at the two splits while the solved split stays between them (flagged; the trace lists both values); a split alternating where the correlation is continuous has its K update under-relaxed instead.
references: Crane Co. TP-410 Flow of Fluids Through Valves, Fittings, and Pipe, 2009.
Silverberg, P., and R. Darby. Correlate pressure drops through fittings. Chem. Eng. 106(7), 1999, 101.
sections.title: Branches

items: Head, efficiency and NPSHr curves: monotone piecewise cubic interpolation (SciPy PchipInterpolator) through the entered points; head and NPSHr are extrapolated along the end slope outside the points (flagged), efficiency is held at its end values (flagged).
Speed: affinity laws, H(Q) = s² H₀(Q/s), NPSHr(Q) = s² NPSHr₀(Q/s), η(Q) = η₀(Q/s).
No viscosity correction: the curves are used as entered for the fluid (the Hydraulic Institute correction, ANSI/HI 9.6.7, is not in this version).
Integral check: a pump closes when the system head exceeds its shutoff head s² H₀(0) or the flow would reverse (EPANET 2.2 pumpstatus), and is flagged as flow reversal.

System curve of a pump: at each flow the pump is replaced by that fixed flow and the network solved, every other element following its own law and status rules (other pumps keep running); the system head is EGL(discharge) − EGL(suction). Default flows: 0 to 1.2 x the curve's largest flow x s. Each point starts from the solution at the neighbouring flow (statuses, branch losses and flows; the first from the network's own solve when the solve computes the curves, from the initial state otherwise), so where the statuses or branch patterns admit more than one solution the curve follows one continuously; a point that fails from there is solved from the initial state, and one that still has no head while the flow has a way through (unless a control valve in series is at its switch, below) is solved again from the initial state (if it did not start there) and from it with its active control valves open, the first solve that gives a head, or finds a control valve in series at its switch, being used (with none, the point keeps its first result) and the next point starting from the result used; a flowing point is not solved again when its flow exceeds what every way from the pump's discharge back to its suction can pass that way (an FCV at most its setpoint, a check valve, PRV, PSV or pump nothing in reverse: a cut, Ford and Fulkerson), since no steady state carries it, and one whose flow is that limit, where every steady state passes each FCV of the cut at its setpoint, is also solved with each such FCV held open, to find whether it sits at its switch. A point has no head where no steady state carries its flow, where its head is undetermined (a side of the pump with no fixed pressure, or a control valve in series at its switch, which could also hold the flow throttled with any higher head) or where its solve does not converge; its message says which. With assigned-flow nodes, the cut counts their flows as fixed demands and supplies (Gale): a demand on the pump's side of the cut takes part of the forced flow, and one beyond it adds to what the cut must pass. Read the other way, the cut bounds the flow from below: a flowing point below the least flow that assigned flows need through the pump (a demand on its discharge side that a one-way element keeps every reservoir and reference node from feeding, or a supply on its suction side that one keeps from draining) has no steady state either and is not solved again, and one at that floor is solved with each FCV of the cut held open too. A side of the pump that reaches only assigned-flow nodes has no point with a head.
references: Fritsch, F. N., and R. E. Carlson. Monotone piecewise cubic interpolation. SIAM J. Numer. Anal. 17(2), 1980, 238-246.

Fritsch, F. N., and J. Butland. A method for constructing local monotone piecewise cubic interpolants. SIAM J. Sci. Stat. Comput. 5(2), 1984, 300-304, doi:10.1137/0905021 (the derivative formula of scipy.interpolate.PchipInterpolator).
Rossman, L. A., et al. EPANET 2.2. US EPA, 2020 (source: src/hydstatus.c, status rules).

Ford, L. R., and D. R. Fulkerson. Maximal flow through a network. Canadian Journal of Mathematics 8, 1956, 399-404 (the max-flow min-cut theorem: the flows no state carries through a pump on its system curve).

Gale, D. A theorem on flows in networks. Pacific Journal of Mathematics 7(2), 1957, 1073-1082 (a flow with fixed supplies and demands exists when no node set holds more net supply than its cut can pass: the assigned flows in a pump's system-curve bounds).
sections.title: Pumps

items: Open valve loss h = K v²/(2g) on the inlet pipe's inner diameter; Cv and Kv converted with fluids.fittings.Cv_to_K / Kv_to_K (ISA-75.01.01, turbulent flow, without the Reynolds number factor F_R); without a resistance, the Crane TP-410 full-bore K for the valve type. A Cv, Kv or Crane K in laminar flow (Re < 2000 in the inlet pipe) is flagged.

Active check valves: open loss h = Δp_crack/(ρg) + K v²/(2g); open above their cracking head and close on reverse flow (EPANET 2.2 cvstatus with the cracking head). A check valve locked open by the user has the open loss K v²/(2g) only, with no cracking head and no check action; locked closed, it passes no flow.

PRV, PSV and FCV hold the outlet static pressure, inlet static pressure or flow when active; status rules from EPANET 2.2 (hydstatus.c) applied to the energy grade line, with the setpoint head z + p/(ρg) + v²/(2g) at the port; an FCV closes on reverse flow (EPANET's would pass it), and an active FCV opens once the head across it is below its fully open loss at the setpoint (EPANET's waits for a reverse head), as the PRV and PSV rules do. Control valves without a resistance: ideal control valve: no loss when fully open (K = 0); give a resistance for a real valve.
Status tolerances: 0.0001 m in head, 1e-08 m³/s in flow.

An active state with no solution falls back to the states the valve rules give at that solve's first iterations (EPANET 2.2 applies them at every iteration), then to open and closed valves (EPANET's badvalve).

A section closed off by closed pumps or valves carries no flow and has no computed pressure; the closed elements around it are re-tested against the heads it can take at zero flow (a dead-headed pump puts its shutoff head on it), and re-opened when no such head keeps them all closed. A PRV or PSV inside such a section or one whose pressure level is undetermined, or closed between two of them, keeps its state only if one set of section levels holds it together with those closed elements and the other such valves; otherwise the fewest of these elements change, each to the state its rule gives at levels that hold the others (a PRV or PSV that could not be active there, with no fixed head to draw from or deliver to, closes if open and opens if closed).
references: Rossman, L. A., et al. EPANET 2.2. US EPA, 2020 (source: src/hydstatus.c, status rules).
ISA-75.01.01-2007 (60534-2-1 Mod), Flow Equations for Sizing Control Valves.
Crane Co. TP-410 Flow of Fluids Through Valves, Fittings, and Pipe, 2009.
sections.title: Valves

items: Pressure relief valves (conventional spring-loaded, liquid service): the lift x rises linearly from 0 at the set pressure difference Δp_s to 1 at full lift, Δp_f = Δp_s (1 + op), and the flow is API 520's liquid capacity equation at that lift, Q = x Kd A √(2 Δp_t/ρ), in exact SI with Kw = Kc = Kv = 1 (API 520's own form rounds its constant to 11.78, 6.09214e-05 above the exact 11.7792823892, which gives that fraction more area for a flow). Δp_t is the total-pressure difference between the ports, (p_in + ρ v_in²/2) − (p_out + ρ v_out²/2) = ρ g (EGL_in − EGL_out − (z_in − z_out)); on the energy grade line the law is h(Q) = h_set + (Δp(Q) − Δp_s)/(ρ g), h_set = Δp_s/(ρ g) + z_in − z_out, with u = √Δp the largest real root of u³ − Δp_s u − R Q = 0 between set and full lift (R = (Δp_f − Δp_s)/(Kd A √(2/ρ)); the increment R Q/u and its slope computed without cancellation) and Δp = ρ Q²/(2 (Kd A)²) from full lift on. h is continuous and strictly increasing, with a finite positive slope at zero flow.

Three named departures. (1) The band between set and full lift is a convention, the linear lift of MathWorks Simscape and AFT Impulse, exact at the two points the certification fixes, not the cited behaviour: Pentair's typical liquid-trim characteristic (TP-V300 Fig. 4-12) lifts to about half at 107 % of set, surges to full lift there, and on falling pressure stays at full lift to about 95 % and recloses near 90 %, so between about 90 % and 107 % of set a real valve has two steady states; a valve that has surged open passes more flow at a lower inlet pressure. No cited source verifies a band law, so every relieving state short of full lift is flagged (CORRELATION_OUT_OF_RANGE, partial lift), and the band is an exception to the project's verifiable gate that the owner accepted (CLAUDE.md D21). (2) API 520's P1 − P2 is read as Δp_t; ASME's definitions as Pentair quotes them (the inlet stagnation pressure, the outlet static pressure) differ by the outlet velocity head, and this reading gives the higher inlet pressure at a given flow. (3) With a superimposed back pressure the overpressure is taken on the set difference, as the opening is, so full lift comes op × the back pressure below the in-situ relieving pressure; at the relieving pressure both readings are at or past full lift and give API 520's flow.

Overpressure at full lift: ASME's liquid certification overpressure, 10 % of the set or 3 psi (20684.3 Pa), whichever is greater (the default), ASME VIII's liquid certification overpressure, for a set of at least 15 psi (103421 Pa), ASME VIII's scope; a certified capacity may give its own. Below that scope the default is not cited: a valve that would take it is refused (RELIEF_VALVE_OUT_OF_RANGE), with the remedy of a certified capacity and its overpressure.

Capacity, one of three kinds, never mixed: an API 526 orifice letter (its effective area) or an API 520 effective area, each with API 520's effective coefficient of discharge 0.65 and ASME's overpressure, for preliminary sizing (an effective area is reported with the smallest API 526 letter covering it, fluids.safety_valve.API520_round_size); or the valve's certified actual orifice area with its rated coefficient of discharge (ASME's K, 0.9 × the measured coefficient) and, optionally, its full-lift overpressure. Pentair: never an effective coefficient or area with a rated coefficient or actual area.

Status: active, or locked closed (gagged, or isolated by its block valve). Its status rule is the check valve's (EPANET 2.2 cvstatus) with the cracking head h_set: at zero flow it opens once the static pressure difference across it exceeds its set by ρ g × 0.0001 m, and it closes on reverse flow. It starts closed, its normal state (a pump deadheaded behind a valve set above its shutoff then runs at zero flow with its shutoff pressure on the inlet). A check valve's cracking pressure, unlike the relief valve's set, is compared with the difference of the energy grade lines. Every closed-off, free-level and system-curve rule applies to it as to a check valve (in a pump's system curve it passes no reverse flow). A point of a pump's system curve, where the pump is a fixed flow, starts it open, as a check valve, so that the flow has its way through it and its rule closes it where the difference across it stays below its set; at zero flow it then sits at its set, H_sys(0) holding h_set.

Flagged: full lift (RELIEF_VALVE_OPEN, information); relieving short of full lift (CORRELATION_OUT_OF_RANGE, partial lift, warning); an active valve closed with a side closed off or on an undetermined level, which has no result (RELIEF_VALVE_CLOSED, information, naming the levels that keep it closed); an outlet whose absolute static pressure is below the vapor pressure while it relieves (BELOW_VAPOR_PRESSURE: the jet would flash, and the flow solved is too high); a liquid of viscosity 0.1 Pa·s or more (CORRELATION_OUT_OF_RANGE, viscosity: API 520's Kv, given in the trace, is not applied). Refused (RELIEF_VALVE_OUT_OF_RANGE): a law the floating point cannot represent (Kd A, Q_f or R not a finite positive normal number), and a set below ASME VIII's scope with ASME's default overpressure.

Not applied: API 520's back-pressure correction Kw (a conventional valve's set is the difference across it), its rupture-disc combination factor Kc and its viscosity correction Kv; no blowdown or pop action; the outlet piping is liquid-full.

sections.title: Relief valves

items: Equipment (one side of a heat exchanger, a coil, a strainer, a filter, or another passive element given by its datasheet): the loss of total head from its inlet to its outlet is h = EGL_in − EGL_out = c Q|Q| (a loss of total pressure ρ g h), with c = ΔP_r/(ρ_r g Q_r²) from the rated pressure drop ΔP_r at the rated flow Q_r for a fluid of density ρ_r: a constant K, the square law of ISA-75.01.01-2007 eq. (1) for non-choked, turbulent liquid flow, and the high-Re limit of the 3-K method (Silverberg & Darby). The rated drop is the dissipative loss (friction and form) of total pressure between the ports, without the static head between them: each port's static pressure follows from its EGL with the velocity in its connected pipe, so the static drop reported is ρ g h + ρ g (z_out − z_in) + ρ (v_out² − v_in²)/2.

Density scaling: the pressure loss at the solved flow is ρ g h = ΔP_r (ρ/ρ_r)(Q/Q_r)², with ρ the fluid being solved. The operating density cancels out of the head loss h, which the rating alone sets; it only converts head to pressure.

A Cv or Kv rating is a rated point on water by definition (1 psi at Cv US gpm, 1 bar at Kv m³/h): c = K/(2 g A²) with K from fluids.fittings.Cv_to_K / Kv_to_K (ISA-75.01.01-2007, water at 999.29744568 kg/m³), the valves' conversion, evaluated at a 1 m bore; K ∝ D⁴ makes K/A² the same on every bore, so no pipe diameter is needed. Its pressure loss is (ρ/ρ_w) × 1 psi × (Q/Cv gpm)², or × 1 bar × (Q/Kv m³/h)².
Reverse flow (outlet → inlet) follows the same, symmetric law and is flagged: no datasheet rates reverse flow.
Laminar flow (Re < 2000) in the end segment of a connected pipe is flagged, as for a valve's Cv or Kv: the square law is the turbulent-flow law, and the loss is then likely underestimated.

At zero flow the law's slope 2c|Q| is 0: Newton's Jacobian uses at least 1e-06 x the slopes of the pipes at the element's ports there, as for every link that is not a pipe (EPANET 2.2 bounds such a gradient instead); the law itself is exact.

Viscosity is not corrected: the loss scales with density only. With a fluid more viscous than the rating's, or at flows well below the rated flow, the real loss may be higher than this law gives (a smooth-tube element dominated by friction scales as ρ^0.75 μ^0.25 Q^1.75 by Blasius' law); a correction needs the equipment's geometry or its vendor's own factors.
references: ISA-75.01.01-2007 (60534-2-1 Mod), Flow Equations for Sizing Control Valves.
Silverberg, P., and R. Darby. Correlate pressure drops through fittings. Chem. Eng. 106(7), 1999, 101.
sections.title: Equipment

items: Orifice plates (square-edged, concentric; a restriction orifice, or a flow meter with pressure taps): the loss of total head from the inlet to the outlet is h = EGL_in − EGL_out = K v|v|/(2g), with v = Q/A in the inlet pipe of inner diameter D (its end segment at the inlet port), β = d/D, and K = (S/(C β²) − 1)², S = √(1 − β⁴(1 − C²)): ISO 5167-2's pressure-loss relation Δϖ = (S − C β²)/(S + C β²) × Δp over ρ v²/2 (fluids.flow_meter.discharge_coefficient_to_K, computed without its cancellation as β → 1). Δϖ = ρ g h is the permanent pressure loss, the part not recovered about 6 D downstream; the outlet port's pressure is the recovered one.

The discharge coefficient C that sets the loss is the one at D and D/2 tappings for every plate, whatever its own taps: ISO 5167-2:2003 eq. (4), the Reader-Harris/Gallagher equation (fluids.flow_meter.C_Reader_Harris_Gallagher), at Re_D = 4ρ|Q|/(πDμ) in the inlet pipe. One plate has one permanent loss; the loss relation's theory (Reader-Harris et al. 2019) takes C with tappings 1D upstream, and of ISO's tap sets only D and D/2 has L1 = 1 (Deltares WANDA makes the same choice). Named departures, each at its largest over ISO 5167-2's range (D 50 mm to 1 m, β 0.1 to 0.75, Re_D from Re_lo up): ISO's relation read with a meter's own C would give a K up to 6.14 % higher at corner tappings and 6.34 % at flange tappings (at β 0.75 as Re_D grows, flange on a 1 m pipe), a flow up to 2.94 % and 3.03 % lower where the plate takes the whole head (up to β 0.6: a K up to 0.64 % and 0.84 % higher, a flow up to 0.32 % and 0.42 % lower); Reader-Harris et al.'s own C, with the downstream pressure at 0.125 D, gives a K 0.063 to 1.24 % lower (a flow up to 0.63 % higher).

Below ISO 5167-2's lowest Reynolds number Re_lo, C is held at its value there and flagged (WANDA's practice; eq. (4) as written exceeds 1 at very low Re): Re_lo = max(5000, 16000 β²) at corner and D and D/2 tappings and max(5000, 170000 β² D) at flange tappings (D in m). The first is ISO's limit (5000 for β ≤ 0.56, 16000 β² above) made continuous at β 0.56, stricter by at most 17.6 for 0.559 < β < 0.56, so that the held loss decreases with β. So fluids is never evaluated below Re 5000, where it adds terms that are not in ISO 5167-2.

A plate whose coefficient that sets the loss, at D and D/2 tappings (ISO's C there, or an entered C moved there from corner or flange taps), could exceed 1 at some flow is refused (ORIFICE_OUT_OF_RANGE): C ≤ 1 is a jet no larger than the bore, and above it K falls below the sudden expansion from the bore (Borda-Carnot), which is physically impossible. So is a plate whose ISO coefficient could exceed 1 where eq. (4) serves only the reading or the move: at its corner or flange tappings for ISO's meter reading, or at either tap set in the ratio that moves an entered C. Eq. (4) is then extrapolated far beyond ISO's range (its largest C there is below 0.7), and the reading or the move would rest on it. Each bound takes each Reynolds-number-dependent term of eq. (4) at whichever end of [Re_lo, ∞) makes it safe. For ISO's C it refuses β from about 0.970 (0.97025 from D 71.12 mm, at most 0.9706 on smaller pipes), and with flange taps on a pipe below about 55 mm, where ISO's C at the flange tappings is the bound, from a lower β (0.969 at D 52.5 mm, 0.963 at 40.9 mm, 0.930 at 15.8 mm, lower still on smaller pipes). A plate whose loss coefficient K/(2 g A²) at its smallest C is not a finite positive floating-point number is refused too.

A meter's reading, the differential pressure between its taps, is ISO 5167-2 eq. (1) solved for Δp with ε = 1: Δp = (1 − β⁴)/(C_M² β⁴) · ρ v|v|/2, with C_M ISO's C at its own taps (held at their own Re_lo) or the entered C; it does not act on the network. A plate without taps (a restriction orifice) has no reading.

The static pressure at the vena contracta, p_vc = p_up + ρ g (z_up − z_down) − (1 − β⁴)/(C² β⁴) · ρ v²/2 (up: the port the flow enters; down: the port it leaves by, at whose elevation it is taken, as in WANDA), is checked against the vapor pressure and flagged where the liquid would flash (BELOW_VAPOR_PRESSURE): a flashing jet chokes the flow, so the flow solved is then too high. None at zero flow or where the pressure level is undetermined; incipient cavitation is not checked.

Flagged (CORRELATION_OUT_OF_RANGE), wherever eq. (4) is used: a bore below 12.5 mm, an inlet pipe outside 50 mm to 1000 mm, β outside 0.1 to 0.75 (ISO 5167-2's limits, from fluids' documentation); and for every plate, an outlet pipe of another bore than the inlet's (the relation assumes the jet recovers in the same bore) and reverse flow (the loss taken as for forward flow at the same flow rate: ISO's C is for flow onto the plate's upstream face). The plate and its installation (edge, thickness, straight lengths, roughness) are assumed to meet ISO 5167-2 and are not checked.

At zero flow the law's slope is 0: Newton's Jacobian uses at least 1e-06 x the slopes of the pipes at the plate's ports there, as for every link that is not a pipe; the law itself is exact. Elsewhere the slope is exact, with the derivative of eq. (4) in the Reynolds number.
ε = 1: the expansibility factor of a liquid.
references: ISO 5167-2:2003, Measurement of fluid flow by means of pressure differential devices inserted in circular cross-section conduits running full, Part 2: Orifice plates; eq. (1), eq. (4) (the Reader-Harris/Gallagher (1998) equation) and the pressure-loss relation, as fluids 1.3.1 implements them (fluids.flow_meter), with its limits from fluids' docstrings (also citing ASME MFC-3M-2004). The 2022 edition does not change eq. (4) or its limits (Reader-Harris, M. J. ISO 5167: Past and Present. Global Flow Measurement Workshop, 2022).

Reader-Harris, M. J., J. Barnett and K. Mistry. Orifice plate pressure loss ratio: theoretical work in compressible flow and experimental work in CO2. FLOMEKO 2019, Lisbon (the loss relation's momentum theory, C taken with tappings 1D upstream and between the plate and the vena contracta downstream, and pressures moved between tap positions with the Reader-Harris/Gallagher (1998) equation).

Deltares. WANDA documentation, ORIFICE component (an orifice plate complying with ISO 5167-2:2003): the loss H1 − H2 for D and D/2 tappings, the Reynolds number held at the standard's minimum, symmetric reverse flow, and the vena-contracta pressure at the downstream side's elevation.

p = ρ g (EGL − z_port − v²/(2g)): static gauge pressure at a port (z_port: the port's elevation; v: the velocity in the pipe connected there, Q/A of its end segment)

notes: Scenario 'Supply at AF1' (id S2) overrides the base project here: assigned flow -0.002 m³/s (base: 0.003 m³/s). The inputs below are the scenario's values.

Assigned-flow node: it fixes the flow at its port whatever the pressure there. It is not a fixed-pressure boundary: a part of the network that no reservoir or reference node reaches through open elements (cut off by a closed valve or a stopped pump, say) carries a nonzero flow only if the assigned flows there sum to zero, and then its flows are solved and its pressure level is not (UNDETERMINED_PRESSURE); otherwise no steady state carries them, and the solve is reported as not converged, naming the node. A zero flow there is a closed end (ISOLATED_SECTION).
